passages.title: Goya's portraits
passages.text:
There are, according to current scholarship, 160 existing portraits by Francisco de Goya, about a third of his painted output. The real number, though, is much greater, since there are no pure landscapes in Goya's work. He was not interested in paintings of nature – everything he ever did deals with people. In the work of no other great portraitist are a nation's people, folk traditions and superstitions so comprehensively and relentlessly captured. Put his work together – the public and private paintings and the personal drawings and sketches – and what you have is a comprehensive portrait of Spain itself. His subject was a good one since Goya lived in fascinating times: his lifetime was a period that saw Spain pass through enormous changes. People were the constant during these unstable times and he recorded both the faces of those who mattered to Spain and to him – often they were one and the same.

His work as a portraitist has its origins in the 45 tapestry cartoons he painted for the Royal Tapestry Factory in Madrid after he moved there in 1775. Although his designs don't show portraits, they do show types of people – the residents of the city who gave Madrid its street swagger: peasants and rich men, courting couples, singers, hunters, children and young men and women playing blind man's buff or tossing a mannequin into the air. The pictures use a limited range of colours, and the faces are individualised without being those of particular people. But in them Goya practised poses and groupings and a way of handling light on and around figures that was to be invaluable.

The tapestry designs show social roles rather than the people inhabiting them, but when it came to painting portraits, Goya would turn this on its head. His greatest strength as a portraitist is that regardless of the status of the sitter, be they a king or a queen, a soldier, a priest or writer, it was the person he showed first and their position second. It was this trait, most apparent in his royal portraiture, which has led him to be seen as satirising the Bourbon monarchy rather than as a painter who depicted what he saw without using the usual flattering conventions. In the art critic Robert Hughes's phrase he did not 'pay reflexive homage to authority' but instead walked a fine line between respect and truth.

Goya's success was rapid: in 1785 he was made deputy director of painting at the Royal Academy (his main message to his students was subversive – 'there are no rules in painting') and in 1786 he became the official court painter, which involved painting 'works required for royal service'. He immediately spent some of his generous salary on a two-wheeled horse carriage (one of only three in Madrid at the time) which he crashed on his first outing. His self-confidence untouched, he wrote to his childhood friend Martin Zapater: “I have now established an enviable way of living: I do not wait on anyone in antechambers, and if anyone wants anything from me they must come to me. I have made myself more in demand and unless it is a person of rank or at the request of a friend I would do nothing for anyone...”

Part of the reason for his success was that, unlike the 18th-century British artist Gainsborough, for example, he did not resent portraiture as an economically necessary chore that ate away at the time he could devote to higher art. Portraiture fascinated him; it was, as he put it, part of that 'sacred science which requires so much study', and his portraits reveal a fully engaged artist. There is hardly any repetition in his poses (he drew on prints of English portraits for inspiration). He worked hard to give his sitters in repose a sense of latent movement and he defined them by the careful depiction of the space around them.

“My work is very simple. My art reveals idealism and truth,” Goya claimed. The truth though is always more apparent than the idealism. With the portrait of Charles IV and the royal family of 1800, one of the most important commissions of his career, Goya rejected entirely the grandeur of majesty to portray the assembled Bourbons as they appeared – a motley grouping in fancy clothes. In fact, a French visitor to the Spanish court had previously likened Charles and his queen Maria Luisa to a butcher and his wife. Goya may have been a political liberal but he wouldn't have jeopardised his hard-won new position as first court painter in order to score political points at the expense of his patrons. That his sitters didn't regard the portrait as unflattering was evidenced by succeeding royal commissions, not least his 1815 portrait of Ferdinand VII. Ferdinand himself was physically unprepossessing, and had a reputation for being tyrannical, vicious and small-minded, so that is exactly how Goya shows him. The king, however, looking in Goya's particular mirror, saw no such characteristics staring back at him.

The private side of Goya's portraiture was a world away from the public. The contrast between the Ferdinand portrait and the remarkable 1820 double portrait showing Goya with Dr Arrieta represents a moral version of three aspects of the human condition. In this portrait, the 73-year-old painter is suffering from a debilitating illness and is being tended by his doctor. If Ferdinand represents human malignity and Goya its frailty then Arrieta stands for man's innate kindness. While not all his portraits are successful (some have a doll-like stiffness), this is what Goya at his best could do: in the guise of representing individuals he showed, without judging, man as a universal being.

passages.title: IQ Scores
passages.text:
Studies from numerous countries suggest that IQ scores have been rising fast since at least the 1950s - enough to mean that someone with an IQ classed as average at that time could be labelled as having low intelligence today. However psychologists disagree about what the upward trend in scores really means. Some researchers argue that people are not getting more intelligent overall, but just getting better at a particular sort of problem solving. Others say they have found echoes of rising IQ scores in ‘real world’ measures of intelligence. To confuse things still more, there are hints that the trend may be about to grind to a halt.

James Flynn, a professor of political science, first showed that IQ scores were rising in the mid-1980s, and became famous after others dubbed the pattern he had observed the 'Flynn effect’. In a landmark paper he made detailed comparisons across fourteen countries of trends in the results of tests that measure reasoning power. Overall, these showed a real growth in scores of up to 25 points in a generation. To find out more, Flynn went on to look at scores for each type of reasoning that IQ tests set out to measure, such as verbal, numerical and visuo-spatial. This last test category usually includes 'Raven's matrices' - sequential patterns with one piece missing. The candidate has to choose, from a set of alternatives, which shape to put in the empty space. When Flynn took a closer look at the scores, the pattern was clear. The strongest gains in almost every case were on Raven’s matrices and similar tests, while verbal and arithmetical scores showed more modest rises. Since presenting his original paper, Flynn has looked at data from further countries and found the same upward trend, with the same skills responsible for most of the increase.

Flynn feels that his eponymous effect is meaningful, but does not interpret it as evidence that people are becoming cleverer. ‘Our grandparents were not retarded and we are not geniuses,’ he says. ‘More likely we have simply developed the skills and habits of mind that make us better at solving abstract problems, and - just as importantly - we take such problems seriously.’ Flynn believes that demands on visuo-spatial abilities have grown because of TV, computers and cars, and also that in societies where intelligence has become something people focus on excessively, abstract problem-solving skills develop faster than other skills.

Others have different views about what might account for the increase in IQ scores. John Rust of the University of London suggests that it is not just an increase in visuo-spatial activities that is pushing up IQ scores. He believes that there are several factors, including the fact that, in more complex societies, people have to think harder to find solutions to problems they face. He also points out that if just one mind grasps a new concept, such as Einstein and the theory of relativity, it may then be easier for society in general to think in a more complex way. Others, such as experimental psychologist Robert Howard, argue that overall intelligence really has risen, helped by better nutrition, smaller families, wider access to education and other environmental changes.

Howard’s latest research has sent him on a different line of enquiry. Controversially, he now believes that the rise in IQ scores might have peaked in industrialised countries. To support this view, he cites data from Denmark. The Danish military still summons virtually all young men before a draft board to identify who is suitable to do military service. Since 1957, all 17-year-olds there have taken exactly the same qualifying IQ tests - including ones similar to Raven's matrices. Candidates must also be able to answer verbal questions such as 'Sun is to day as Moon is to ?' and number-series questions such as '2,3,5,8,?'. Results in these tests have been carefully analysed by Thomas Teasdale, a neuropsychologist. He found that during the 1960s and '70s, scores showed gains on a scale similar to those of other countries, but by the 1990s the rate of improvement had slowed right down to about one IQ point over the decade. Furthermore, the scores were improving only on the visuo-spatial questions; verbal and numerical performance was flattening out. Most intriguingly, however, scores from 1999 onwards show an overall downturn. One explanation might be that there is some absolute ceiling to people’s abilities to perform these tasks, no matter how much the prevailing culture encourages them. However, as Teasdale points out, if such a ceiling had been reached, the test results should show scores pushing against it rather than actually falling.

Flynn is keeping a close eye on the findings, but is not jumping to conclusions until data from other countries is available. However, he does wonder whether the conditions leading to dramatic improvements in mental ability disappear as societies become more prosperous. He points out that in human history, prosperity often led to decadence, and argues that the case of ancient Rome can be viewed as an illustration of this.

passages.title: Grimms’ Fairy Tales
passages.text:
In the early 19th century, the brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm began collecting folktales for a book of fairy tales that would enchant millions in faraway places for generations to come. They named their story collection Children’s and Household Tales and published the first edition in Germany in 1812. Grimms’ Fairy Tales, as the English-language version is usually called, now belong to world culture. So far the collection has been translated into more than 160 languages. The stories and their characters continue to appear in virtually all media: theatre, opera, comic books, movies, paintings, rock music, advertising, fashion. The Japanese have built two theme parks devoted to the tales. In the United States the Grimms’ stories helped launch Walt Disney as a media giant.

Such lasting fame would have shocked the humble Grimms. During their lifetimes the collection sold modestly in Germany, at first only a few hundred copies a year. The early editions were not even aimed at children. The brothers initially refused to consider illustrations, and scholarly footnotes took up almost as much space as the tales themselves. Jacob and Wilhelm viewed themselves as patriotic collectors of folklore, rather than entertainers of children. They began their work at a time when Germany had been overrun by the French under Napoleon. The new rulers were intent on suppressing local culture. As young, hard-working scholars, the brothers undertook the fairy tale collection with the goal of saving the endangered oral tradition of Germany.

The brothers were initially assisting a friend who planned to publish a collection of German folk literature. But when the friend failed to produce the collection, the brothers decided to publish their own volume. For much of the 19th century, teachers and parents, particularly in the United States, deplored the Grimms’ collection for its uncivilized content. Offended adults objected to the gruesome punishments inflicted on the stories’ villains. In the original ‘Snow White’ the evil stepmother is forced to dance in red-hot iron shoes until she falls down dead. Even today some protective parents steer clear of the Grimms’ tales because of this reputation.

Despite its sometimes rocky reception, Children’s and Household Tales gradually became accepted. The appearance of the Grimms’ collection in the 19th century coincided with a great flowering of children’s literature in Europe. Newly literate parents were seeking virtuous material for the nursery and publishers, led by those in England, rushed to meet the demand, issuing high-quality picture books and folktale collections. Once the Grimms sighted this new public, they set about refining and softening their tales.

In the 20th century the Grimms’ fairy tales dominated the bookshelves of children’s bedrooms. And why not? The stories read like dreams come true: handsome lads and beautiful maidens, armed with magic, triumph over giants and witches and wild beasts. They outwit mean, selfish adults. Inevitably the boy and girl fall in love and live happily ever after. And parents keep reading because they approve of lessons inserted into the stories: Keep your promises, don’t talk to strangers, work hard, obey your parents.

Together some 40 persons delivered tales to the Grimms. One of these was Dorothea Viehmann, an innkeeper’s daughter, who had grown up listening to stories from travelers who stayed at the inn. Among her treasures was ‘Cinderella’. Another was Marie Hassenpflug from a French-speaking family, who was credited with narrating many of the most famous tales. Her stories blended motifs from the oral tradition and from Perrault’s influential 1697 book, Tales of My Mother Goose, which contained versions of ‘Little Red Riding Hood,’ ‘Snow White,’ and ‘Sleeping Beauty’. These stories had been adapted from earlier Italian fairy tales. In the second edition of their own collection the Grimms acknowledged the deep international roots of many of their tales. Included in their notes are references to variants from many other cultures, including Russian, Finnish, Japanese, Irish, and Slavic.

Given that the origins of many of the Grimms’ fairy tales reach throughout Europe and into the Middle East and Orient, the question must be asked: How German are the Grimms’ tales? Very, says scholar Heinz Rölleke. Love of the underdog and rural simplicity – these are German traits. Throughout Europe children were often neglected and abandoned, like Hansel and Gretel. Accused witches were burned at the stake, like the evil mother-in-law in ‘The Six Swans’. ‘The cruelty in the stories was not the Grimms’ fantasy,’ Rölleke points out. ‘It reflected the law-and-order system of those times.’

The tales may reflect the specific values of 19th-century German society, but that has not stopped the tales from being embraced by almost every culture and nationality in the world. What accounts for this widespread, enduring popularity? Bernhard Lauer points to the ‘universal style’ of the writing. ‘You have no concrete descriptions of the land, or the clothes, or the forest, or the castles. It makes the stories timeless and placeless.’ According to Jack Zipes ‘the tales show a striving for happiness that none of us knows but that we sense is possible. We can identify with the heroes of the tales and become in our mind the masters and mistresses of our own destinies.’ Bruno Bettelheim promoted the therapeutic value of the Grimms’ stories. By confronting fears and phobias, symbolized by witches, heartless stepmothers, and hungry wolves, children find they can master their anxieties. This adaptability of interpretation makes these tales relevant across nearly every era and culture.

passages.title: Traditional Maori Fish Hooks
passages.text:
Effective fish hooks were used by Maori to harvest the rich fisheries of New Zealand, but after the introduction of metals by Europeans they were quickly discarded. The nature of the designs, their function and unrecognised benefits were lost, and subsequently many hooks were incorrectly interpreted as decorative, ceremonial or superstitious objects. So it is ironic that internationally many commercial fishermen now regard circle hooks as a recent innovation, even though they were the preferred design used by Maori centuries ago.

Maori, who had always been great fishermen, first sailed to New Zealand from the Pacific islands between 1250 and 1300 AD. However, in the new country they found different types of wood, bone and stone from those they were familiar with from the tropical Pacific islands, so they set about adapting and revising the skills they used to fabricate the hooks – known as 'matau' – and other tackle needed to harvest fish. It has also been found that New Zealand plants such as flax, cabbage tree and astelia provided fibrous material for fishing lines and nets that was equal to, or superior to, the jute, hemp and sisal in use by Europeans at the time. But unlike metals that can be forged or bent into any desired shape, the materials available to Maori imposed limitations on hook design because of the nature of their structure, and compromises were necessary.

The first European explorers in New Zealand often observed local fishing techniques and seem to have come into possession of some fishing equipment, as various hooks were returned to Europe and displayed. The explorers, however, were not overly impressed, writing that Maori hooks were 'odd', 'of doubtful efficacy', or 'very clumsy affairs'. Even recent archaeologists have commented that the traditional hook was 'shaped in a manner which looks most ineffective for catching fish'. William Anderson, the surgeon on board the Resolution during Captain Cook's third voyage to New Zealand in 1777, remarked on the great productivity of Maori intensive agriculture, but was perplexed by their 'wooden fish hooks pointed with bone, which are so oddly made that a stranger cannot understand how they can be successful.'

Two hundred and thirty years later, a study of Maori fish hooks undertaken by Victoria University showed that the unusual design was related to how the hooks functioned - catching fish by rotating away from the direction of the point and becoming wedged under the jaw, rather than penetrating the side of the fish's mouth in the manner of a European hook, or by acting as a lever as proposed by some archaeologists.

Maori were quick to adopt new materials that became available after the arrival of Europeans in the late 1700s. They continued to make fish hooks according to their traditional designs, but used the new metals and imported fibres. The more commonplace traditional hooks were either thrown away, after which the wooden and flax components soon decomposed, or were used to acquire blankets or medicines from Europeans, with the result that a regular trade developed. More highly prized fish hooks made from ivory or greenstone were often retained and used for jewellery, and today stylised fish hooks are seen as a symbol of Maori cultural revival.

But despite the arrival of new materials, Maori continued to replicate traditional forms in preference to hook shapes introduced by Europeans well into the late 1800s. Eventually, however, the extraordinary quantity of mass-produced metal European hooks being brought into the country led to a significant reduction in their cost, making them irresistible to Maori. This, and the difficulty of manufacturing traditional designs from nails and the other metal objects available to Maori, diminished the use of traditional designs. However, in the late 1800s and early 1900s, the increasing demand for Maori artefacts in Europe, in particular from collectors who were fascinated by Pacific cultures, led to heightened interest in fish hooks. One consequence of this was the increasing incidence of Maori manufacturing fake hooks for sale into this lucrative market. These can usually be identified by the quality of their construction and carving, or by the materials used.

In many ways the evolution of Maori fish hooks mirrors the way in which Maori adapted many European materials and technologies to their own purpose. European influence and technology added to, rather than replaced, generally compatible Maori techniques. This is relevant to fish hooks but also many other aspects of Maori life, in particular the development of various tools, where customary materials were replaced or complemented by metals and, more recently, synthetic materials. Today, commercial boats around the world have adopted a circular hook design because it has proved more effective. Closer inspection shows that these hooks are almost identical in form and function to the traditional matau - technology preferred by Maori since their arrival in New Zealand.
passages.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions below.

questions.prompt: The purpose of Maori hooks was sometimes misunderstood.
questions.explanation: 文章指出，人们遗忘了鱼钩的设计和功能后，把许多鱼钩误解为装饰、仪式或迷信用品。题干所说的用途被误解，正对应incorrectly interpreted。

evidence.quote: many hooks were incorrectly interpreted as decorative, ceremonial or superstitious objects.
evidence.translation: 许多鱼钩被错误地理解为装饰品、仪式用品或迷信物件。

questions.questionTranslation: 毛利鱼钩的用途有时会被误解。

questions.prompt: Fishing was more difficult in New Zealand than in the Pacific Islands.
questions.explanation: 文章说新西兰的木材、骨材和石材不同，毛利人因此需要调整渔具制作技艺，但没有比较两地实际捕鱼的难度。材料不同不能直接推出捕鱼更困难。

evidence.quote: they found different types of wood, bone and stone from those they were familiar with from the tropical Pacific islands
evidence.translation: 他们发现了与熟悉的热带太平洋岛屿不同的木材、骨材和石材。

questions.questionTranslation: 在新西兰捕鱼比在太平洋岛屿捕鱼更困难。

questions.prompt: After moving to New Zealand, Maori used new materials for making fishing equipment.
questions.explanation: 迁居新西兰后，毛利人面对不同的当地材料，调整了制作鱼钩和其他渔具的技艺；文章还列举了用于钓线和渔网的新西兰植物纤维。这支持采用新材料制作渔具的说法。

evidence.quote: they set about adapting and revising the skills they used to fabricate the hooks – known as 'matau' – and other tackle needed to harvest fish.
evidence.translation: 他们开始调整和改进制作技艺，用来制造称为“matau”的鱼钩，以及捕捞鱼类所需的其他渔具。

questions.questionTranslation: 迁居新西兰后，毛利人采用了新的材料制作渔具。

questions.prompt: Maori fishing line was poor quality compared to that used by Europeans.
questions.explanation: 文章说毛利钓线和渔网的植物纤维材料，与欧洲人使用的材料相当或更好。题干却说质量较差，与equal to, or superior to的比较方向相反。

evidence.quote: fibrous material for fishing lines and nets that was equal to, or superior to, the jute, hemp and sisal in use by Europeans at the time.
evidence.translation: 用于钓线和渔网的纤维材料，其品质不亚于、甚至优于当时欧洲人使用的黄麻、大麻和剑麻。

questions.questionTranslation: 与欧洲人使用的钓线相比，毛利人的钓线质量较差。

questions.prompt: The shape of Maori hooks was restricted by the materials used.
questions.explanation: 金属可以按需要锻打和弯曲，但毛利人原先可用的材料受到自身结构限制，鱼钩设计必须因此折中。题干restricted对应imposed limitations。

evidence.quote: the materials available to Maori imposed limitations on hook design because of the nature of their structure
evidence.translation: 毛利人能够获得的材料因自身结构特点而限制了鱼钩的设计。

questions.questionTranslation: 毛利鱼钩的形状受到所用材料的限制。

questions.prompt: Early European explorers were given fish hooks as gifts by Maori.
questions.explanation: 文章说探险家似乎获得了一些渔具，并把鱼钩带回欧洲展示，但没有说明获取方式是赠送、交换还是其他途径。拥有鱼钩这一结果不足以证明它们是礼物。

evidence.quote: seem to have come into possession of some fishing equipment, as various hooks were returned to Europe and displayed.
evidence.translation: 他们似乎获得了一些渔具，因为各种鱼钩被带回欧洲展示。

questions.questionTranslation: 早期欧洲探险家获得了毛利人作为礼物赠送的鱼钩。

questions.prompt: At the time of William Anderson's visit, Maori were already engaged in the growing of crops.
questions.explanation: Anderson来访时称赞毛利集约农业的高生产力，这表明当地当时已经开展农作物种植。虽然他不理解鱼钩的效果，但这不影响关于农业的明确观察。

evidence.quote: remarked on the great productivity of Maori intensive agriculture
evidence.translation: 称赞了毛利集约农业的高生产力。

questions.questionTranslation: William Anderson来访时，毛利人已经在种植农作物。

questions.prompt: The Victoria study showed that Maori and European hooks worked in similar ways.
questions.explanation: 研究将两种鱼钩的工作方式明确区分：毛利鱼钩通过旋转卡住鱼下颌，欧洲鱼钩则刺穿鱼嘴侧面。题干说两者相似，与这一机制对比相反。

evidence.quote: catching fish by rotating away from the direction of the point and becoming wedged under the jaw, rather than penetrating the side of the fish's mouth in the manner of a European hook
evidence.translation: 鱼钩朝背离钩尖所指的方向旋转，卡在鱼的下颌下方，从而钩住鱼，而不是像欧洲鱼钩那样刺穿鱼嘴侧面。

questions.questionTranslation: 维多利亚大学的研究表明，毛利鱼钩和欧洲鱼钩的工作方式相似。

questions.prompt: Valuable hooks were kept as________
questions.explanation: 普通鱼钩被丢弃或用于交换，象牙和绿玉等珍贵鱼钩则保留下来当首饰。题干valuable对应highly prized，填jewellery；同一不可数名词的美式拼写jewelry也可以。

evidence.quote: More highly prized fish hooks made from ivory or greenstone were often retained and used for jewellery
evidence.translation: 更珍贵的象牙或绿玉鱼钩常被保留下来当作首饰。

passages.title: Songs of Ourselves
passages.text:
Surprisingly, music is one of the few abilities that all humans have in common. Any individual from Stone Age tribesman to suburban teenager has the ability to recognize and make music without training. Why this should be so is a bit of a mystery. After all, music isn't necessary for survival. Language, however, is. With language, members of a tribe can organize a migration across Africa and communicate at night without seeing each other. No other animal has managed to develop this capacity and preference for manipulating symbols and syntax to such a refined extent.

Scientists have always been intrigued by the connection between music and language but, over time, words and melody have acquired a vastly different status. Language has long been considered essential to unlocking the mechanisms of man's brainpower. Music, however, is generally treated as a trivial aspect of evolution — mere 'auditory cheesecake', as the Harvard cognitive scientist Steven Pinker puts it. However, recent publications suggest that language and music may equally be able to tell us who we are and where we are from — emotionally and biologically.

To grasp the originality of this idea, it's necessary to realize how music has traditionally been understood. First, musicologists have long emphasized that while each country stamps its identity onto music, music itself has some universal qualities. For example, in most countries sound is divided into the 12 intervals that make up the chromatic scale — that is, the scale represented by the keys on the piano.

For centuries, observers have attributed this preference for certain combinations of tones to the mathematical properties of sound itself. Some 2,500 years ago, the Greek philosopher Pythagoras noted a direct relationship between the pleasing quality of a tone combination and the physical dimensions of the object producing it. For example, a plucked string plays an octave lower than a similar string half its size. This relation between music and maths is often accompanied by the notion, espoused by Charles Rosen, that music exists apart from the world in which it was created. Painting and sculpture, on the other hand, reproduce at least some aspects of nature, and writing describes familiar thoughts and feelings.

Neither idea is right, according to a recent study carried out by David Schwartz, Catherine Howe and Dale Purves. Human predilections towards music are fundamentally shaped not by elegant algorithms or ratios, but by the messy sounds of real life and of speech, in particular. Schwartz, Howe and Purves analyzed a vast selection of speech sounds to reveal the patterns common to all utterances. Using a database of over 100,000 brief segments of speech, they noted which frequency had the greatest emphasis in each sound and discovered that the resulting frequencies corresponded closely to the chromatic scale. In short, the building blocks of music are to be found in speech.

Far from being abstract, music presents a strange analog to the patterns created by the sounds of speech. 'Music, like the visual arts, is rooted in our experience of the natural world,' says Schwartz. 'It emulates our sound environment in the way that visual arts emulate the visual environment.' In music, we hear the echo of our basic sound-making instrument — the vocal tract. The explanation for human music is simple: we like the sounds that are familiar to us — specifically, we like the sounds that remind us of us.

Schwartz's study also illuminates the long-running debate as to whether animals understand or enjoy music. Despite the apparent abundance of music in the natural world, previous studies have found that many laboratory animals don't show a great affinity for human music. Marc Hauser and Josh McDermott of Harvard argued in Nature Neuroscience that animals don't create or hear music the way we do. The fact that some laboratory monkeys show awareness of human tunes is evidence, they say, of shared features of the auditory system, not any specific chimpanzee musical ability.

As for birds, they generally recognize their own narrow repertoire, but don't generate novel melodies like we do. There are no avian Mozarts. But what has been played to the animals, Schwartz notes, is human music. If animals evolve preferences for sound as we do — based upon the soundscape in which they live — then a cat's idea of a good tune would derive from yowls and meows. To demonstrate that animals don't enjoy sounds the way we do, we'd need evidence that they don't respond to 'music' constructed from their own sound environment. To date we don't have this evidence.

No matter how the connection between language and music is explained, what is apparent is that our sense of music, even our love for it, is as deeply rooted in our biology and brains as language is. This is most obvious with babies, says Sandra Trehub in Nature Neuroscience. For babies, music and speech are on a continuum. Mothers use musical speech to 'regulate infants' emotional states', Trehub says. Regardless of what language they speak, the voice all mothers use with babies is the same: 'something between speech and song'. This kind of interaction 'puts the baby in a trance-like state, which may proceed to sleep or extended periods of rapture'. So if the babies of the world could understand the latest research on language and music, they probably wouldn't be very surprised. 'The upshot,' says Trehub, 'is we probably don't realize just how much of a necessity music is.'

passages.title: William Gilbert and magnetism
passages.text:
There was no single moment in history when science replaced mysticism as a means of explaining the workings of the world; but the lives of two men neatly circumscribe the transition, which occurred more or less as the sixteenth century became the seventeenth. After the first decade of the seventeenth century, the modern scientific method had been clearly expressed in the work of the Englishman William Gilbert and the Italian Galileo Galilei, one of the towering figures in science. Gilbert, however, is less well known than he deserves.

William Gilbert's birth predated that of Galileo and, chronologically speaking at least, Gilbert deserves the title of the first scientist. He was born in 1544 in Colchester, a town in south-east England, where he was a member of a prominent local family - his father was an important officer of local government. William had a comfortable place in a settled society; he studied at the local grammar school, then at the University of Cambridge from 1558 until 1569. After that he travelled on the Continent for several years, before settling in London, where he became a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1573.

Gilbert was an extremely successful and eminent doctor, who held just about every office in the Royal College in turn, culminating in his election as President in 1599. The following year, he was appointed as the personal physician of the Queen, Elizabeth I, and was later knighted by her. When she died in May 1603 he was appointed as physician by her successor, King James. But Gilbert outlived Elizabeth by only a few months, dying in December 1603.

In spite of his fame as a medical man, Gilbert made his mark on science in physics, through his thorough investigation of the nature of magnetism. At first he was interested in chemistry, but, after realising that the alchemical belief in the transmutation of metals was nothing but a fantasy, he soon switched to the study of electricity and magnetism, a feature of the world which had remained essentially neglected since the investigations (or rather, speculations) of the Greek philosophers some 2000 years earlier. This work culminated in 1600, after some eighteen years of study, with the publication of a great book, Concerning Magnetism, Magnetic Bodies, and the Great Magnet Earth. It was the first significant work in the physical sciences to be produced in England.

Gilbert's work was comprehensive and thorough. He disproved, by experiment, many old mystical beliefs about magnetism - such as the notion that lodestone, a naturally occurring magnetic ore, could cure headaches, and the idea that a magnet could be deactivated by rubbing with garlic - and invented the technique of magnetising pieces of metal using lodestone. He discovered the laws of magnetic attraction and repulsion that are so familiar to us today from school, showed that the Earth itself acts like a giant bar magnet, and gave the names 'north pole' and 'south pole' to the two extremities of a bar magnet. His investigations were so thorough and complete that, after Gilbert, nothing new was added to scientific knowledge of magnetism for two centuries, until the discovery of electromagnetism in the 1820s and the subsequent work of Michael Faraday.

Gilbert's interests also extended, necessarily in a more speculative way, into the heavens. He was a supporter of the Copernican world model, partly because he thought that the planets might be held in their orbits by magnetism. But Gilbert's originality also shone through in his discussion of Copernican astronomy, where he pointed out how easy it was to explain a certain phenomenon in terms of the wobble of a spinning Earth (like the wobble of a spinning top), and how difficult it was to explain it within the prevailing astronomical theory of crystal spheres centred on the Earth. He also suggested that the stars were not equidistant from the Earth (and not all attached to a single crystal sphere) and might be Sun-like bodies orbited by their own habitable planets. His investigation of static electricity, produced by rubbing objects made of things like amber or glass with silk, was less complete than his study of magnetism. However, Gilbert realised that there was a distinction between electricity and magnetism (indeed, he coined the term 'electric' in this context), although it was not until the 1730s that the French physicist Du Fay discovered that there are two kinds of electric charge, dubbed 'positive' and 'negative', which behave in some ways like magnetic poles, with like charges repelling one another and opposite charges attracting one another.

The most important feature of Concerning Magnetism, though, was not what Gilbert had discovered, but how he had discovered it, and the clear way in which he set out this scientific method as an example for others to follow. He has been described as the founder of the experimental method of science. Gilbert argues 'how very easy it is to make mistakes and errors in the absence of trustworthy experiments', as opposed to the old 'philosophical' approach of trying to understand the workings of the world by pure logic and reason.

passages.title: The controversy about the origins of money – did it really originate from bartering?
passages.titleZh: 关于货币起源的争论：货币真的源于物物交换吗？
passages.text:
The arguments put forward by Alfred Mitchell-Innes in a paper entitled What is Money?, published in the 1913 edition of The Banking Law Journal, have only relatively recently attracted the attention they deserve. In this paper, Mitchell-Innes, a British diplomat then living in the US, reviewed the history and usage of money. On both historical and logical grounds, he asserted that the modern science of political economy rested on a series of assumptions regarding money and credit that were false. One of the most important of these assumptions was the belief that in primitive societies, before the invention of money and a banking system, people relied on barter: exchanging goods and services instead of buying or selling them. This theory about the existence of a barter economy had been the commonly held view ever since it was promoted by the renowned Scottish economist Adam Smith in his 1776 work The Wealth of Nations.

Adam Smith’s explanation appears in countless textbooks on economics, partly because it is a convenient story that seems to make sense to students. This has helped to transform the myth of the barter system into historical fact. It goes something like this. Long ago, before the invention of money, goods were simply traded for other goods. Without money, trade was only possible if there is a double coincidence of needs. If one person grows and sells potatoes and the other makes shoes, they will only engage in exchange if the one selling shoes needs potatoes and the one selling potatoes needs a new pair of shoes.

The problem with this barter system is that, even if they each have a surplus of the goods they wish to sell, no trade will occur unless the potential buyer has something which the seller needs. For Smith, it seemed logical that people had to deal with this problem by using a specific commodity—perhaps gold or silver—to serve as money that could be used to purchase other goods and services. Economists refer to this monetary function as a “medium of exchange”. The need for money becomes even more apparent when dealing with perishable goods such as bread or meat. For example, a butcher may have more meat in his shop than he can consume. If he doesn’t find someone to buy his meat, his meat will spoil. For Smith and his followers, this illustrates the need for money as a means of storing wealth, as well as a medium of exchange. For example, if the butcher could exchange his excess meat for money, he could spend that money one month or one year later when he finally needed more shoes. Even more importantly, once a butcher can exchange his excess meat for money, he is encouraged to work harder, longer, and more efficiently so as to produce more and more excess meat that he can exchange for more money that will store the value of his excess production safely. The implication of this argument is that without money, it would be inefficient and even unwise to over-produce, since most over-production would simply go to waste. It has seemed unjustifiably logical to many economists that money is therefore conducive and even necessary to foster hard work, over-production, profits and a prosperous society.

It was this traditional story that Mitchell-Innes challenged over one hundred years ago. He asserted that the barter theory that emerged from Smith contradicts both logic and historical fact. Smith’s theory simply does not describe what happens in the real world. For example, if you grew up in a small town in the US in the 1970s, you might remember that you could go to the grocery store, pick up groceries, and simply sign a slip of paper acknowledging your receipt of the groceries. The same could be done in Smith’s imagined scenario. If the shoe buyer was trustworthy, the shoe seller could simply create a record of the shoes purchased on credit by the shoe buyer, and of their value in some agreed unit of account. This is certainly not barter, and it is not a purchase using a medium of exchange. Instead it is the exchange of a commodity for a credit.

Although Mitchell-Innes’s work received some favourable reviews at the time, most notably from John Maynard Keynes, the influential British economist, his ideas were neglected for almost 75 years until the 1990s. Since then, academic studies in economics and anthropology demonstrate that there has been a shift in thinking. Some economists now even claim that Smith’s idea was only ever a crude model used to simplify the context of modern economic systems, not a real theory about past ones. Despite all this, incomprehensibly, the myth continues into the 21st century, and still features in economics textbooks and the public’s consciousness.

In his book Debt, the first 5000 years, anthropologist David Graeber asserts that where instances of barter have occurred, it wasn’t as part of a purely barter economy, and money didn’t emerge from it—rather, barter emerged from money. After the fall of the Roman Empire around fifteen hundred years ago, for example, Europeans used barter as a substitute for the Roman currency people had become used to. “In most of the cases we know about, [barter] takes place between people who are familiar with the use of money, but for one reason or another, don’t have a lot of it around,” explains Graeber. He and other anthropologists provide strong arguments which state that many of the examples used by economists in the past to support the view that money originated from bartering were not based on any real evidence. Caroline Humphrey’s paper on barter is regarded as the definitive anthropological work on barter. Her statement is as clear as it is emphatic. “No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money; all available evidence suggests there has never been such a thing.” Mitchell-Innes knew this over a century ago, yet the myth persists.

evidence.translation: 尽管如此，令人难以理解的是，这一未经证实的说法延续到了21世纪，仍出现在经济学教材中，也仍存在于公众的观念中。

questions.questionTranslation: 很难理解为什么21世纪的人们仍相信Smith关于物物交换的观点。

questions.prompt: The bartering economy which emerged after the fall of the Roman Empire was more successful than previous bartering systems.
questions.explanation: 例子说明人们在货币短缺时用物物交换替代旧货币，没有比较它与此前制度的成功程度。发生在较晚时期不等于更成功。

evidence.location: 第6段，第2句（相关范围，不是缺失信息的直接证据）
evidence.quote: After the fall of the Roman Empire around fifteen hundred years ago, for example, Europeans used barter as a substitute for the Roman currency people had become used to.
evidence.translation: 例如，大约1500年前罗马帝国灭亡后，欧洲人用物物交换来代替此前已习惯使用的罗马货币。

evidence.location: 第6段，第3句（相关范围，不是缺失信息的直接证据）
evidence.quote: “In most of the cases we know about, [barter] takes place between people who are familiar with the use of money, but for one reason or another, don’t have a lot of it around,” explains Graeber.
evidence.translation: Graeber 解释说：“在我们所了解的大多数案例中，[物物交换]发生在熟悉货币使用、但出于某种原因手头没有多少货币的人之间。”

questions.questionTranslation: 罗马帝国灭亡后出现的物物交换经济，比此前的物物交换制度更成功。

questions.prompt: Some of the claims made by anthropologists about bartering are easy to dismiss.
questions.explanation: 作者用strong arguments、definitive以及clear...emphatic肯定本段呈现的人类学研究，立场与“很容易驳倒”相反。本题在全文所讨论的这些论断范围内作判断，不把some抽离语境扩大到未提及的其他人类学主张。

evidence.quote: He and other anthropologists provide strong arguments which state that many of the examples used by economists in the past to support the view that money originated from bartering were not based on any real evidence.
evidence.translation: 他和其他人类学家提出了有力论据，指出经济学家过去用来支持“货币源于物物交换”观点的许多例子，并没有任何真实证据作为基础。

evidence.quote: Caroline Humphrey’s paper on barter is regarded as the definitive anthropological work on barter.
evidence.translation: Caroline Humphrey 关于物物交换的论文，被视为这一领域的权威人类学研究。

evidence.quote: Her statement is as clear as it is emphatic.
evidence.translation: 她的表述既清楚又坚决。

evidence.quote: “No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money; all available evidence suggests there has never been such a thing.”
evidence.translation: “从来没有人描述过一个纯粹物物交换经济的实例，更不用说货币从中产生的过程；所有现有证据都表明，这种经济从未存在过。”

questions.questionTranslation: 人类学家关于物物交换的一些论断很容易被驳倒。

questions.prompt: Caroline Humphrey’s claims about bartering oppose those of David Graeber.
questions.explanation: Graeber否定纯粹物物交换经济产生货币的说法，Humphrey同样指出没有这种经济及其产生货币的实例；两者相互支持，不能把Graeber承认货币之后的个别交换读成承认纯粹的前货币经济。

evidence.quote: In his book Debt, the first 5000 years, anthropologist David Graeber asserts that where instances of barter have occurred, it wasn’t as part of a purely barter economy, and money didn’t emerge from it—rather, barter emerged from money.
evidence.translation: 人类学家 David Graeber 在其著作《Debt, the first 5000 years》中指出：即使确实出现过物物交换，也不是发生在纯粹的物物交换经济中；并非货币起源于物物交换，恰恰相反，是物物交换产生于货币使用之后。

evidence.quote: “No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money; all available evidence suggests there has never been such a thing.”
evidence.translation: “从来没有人描述过一个纯粹物物交换经济的实例，更不用说货币从中产生的过程；所有现有证据都表明，这种经济从未存在过。”

questions.questionTranslation: Caroline Humphrey关于物物交换的论断与David Graeber相对立。
